job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Uma Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior financial analyst in the pricing team at Norbury Mutual, an insurance company, and I've been there four months. Mornings I update claims and premium models in spreadsheets, and in the afternoon I help my manager, Sunil, prepare a monthly report on which products are losing money. I did business and finance at a regional university and finished top of my year, and one internship was at a brokerage. I rent a room in a house with two other young professionals. My younger sister Lucia is in her second year of medical school, and my parents are stretching to help her, so I send a bit home when I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but oversold, and I'd tell my colleagues I'd like to see the numbers before anyone changes the way we work. I use an assistant now and then for formulas and drafting, and it saves me time. I'd share that on a team chat, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel fine. Insurance is a trust business, and the people who sign the policies still want somebody they can call and blame when a claim goes wrong. The tools make my afternoons faster, and that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do well, finish the actuarial-lite course my company pays for, and keep using the assistant now and then. I'd save about £250 a month and send £80 home for Lucia's books. I'd also ask Sunil to give me one new model to own each quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. A bit lucky too, because I know a few people who are struggling to find any entry job at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or worry in your own life would stay exactly the same even if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family money: Lucia's fees keep rising, and my parents don't say how tight it is, but I can tell. That's what I worry about, much more than software. It doesn't go away if AI is hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your week is routine screen work that even a small change could touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe half my week is spreadsheet work, so some of it does get touched, mostly the dull formulas. But the report and the judgement calls stay human. If the dull part shrinks, I might get more interesting work sooner.

say: I'd ask to see the **numbers** before anyone changes how we work.
I'd mention on the team chat that the assistant saves me **time**.
think: Insurance is a **trust business** and customers still want a person.
I know graduates who can't find **any** entry job, so I feel lucky.
My worry is **family money**, not software.
do: Finish the actuarial course my **company** pays for.
Save **£250 a month** and send £80 home for Lucia.
Ask Sunil for one new **model** to own each quarter.
feel: A background **tug** about my family's money.
S0.quote: Insurance is a trust business, and the people who sign the policies still want somebody they can call and blame when a claim goes wrong.
fieldNote: She asks for **evidence** before opinion, which shows in everything she says.
Her real pressure is **family** money, her sister's medical fees.
Calm follows from steady work and a **employer-paid** course.

steps.text: Finish the company's actuarial course this year
Use the assistant for formulas and drafts, checking each result
Save £250 a month and send £80 home for Lucia

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should pilot it on a few products and measure the result, not roll it out everywhere. I'd tell friends it's like the spreadsheet in the 1990s: the people who learned it did better. Online, I'd probably stay quiet, because I'd want more evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit nervous about junior roles. If the software drafts the pricing report that I draft now, Sunil will ask why the team needs four analysts and not two. I'd like to be one of the two, but I'm the newest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools more, on purpose, until I'm the person on my team who knows what they do well and badly. I'd ask Sunil if I can lead a pilot. I'd also keep a record of the work I've done, so I can show value in a review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little unsettled, in a manageable way. I'd say I'm curious more than afraid. I don't like not knowing, and it's early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think of a task you did last week. Which part would software take over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The monthly report. Last month I spent two days building and checking it, and the assistant could produce a first draft in an hour. The judgement stays with us: which products to drop and why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your manager do differently about hiring people at your level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd say we'll hold the team size, and over two years it would shrink by not replacing leavers. Sunil would be fair about it, but he reports to a director who reads cost charts. I'd keep an eye on the budget meetings.

say: I'd say we should **pilot** it on a few products and measure.
I'd compare it to the **spreadsheet** in the 1990s.
I'd stay **quiet** online until there is more evidence.
think: I'm nervous about **junior roles**, and I'm the newest.
I want to be one of the **two** analysts kept, not the four.
do: Use the tools **on purpose** until I know their strengths and limits.
Ask Sunil if I can lead a **pilot**.
Keep a record of my **work** for reviews.
S1.quote: If the software drafts the pricing report that I draft now, Sunil will ask why the team needs four analysts and not two.
fieldNote: She wants to **lead** the pilot, so she shapes the change rather than reacts.
Measured tone: evidence first, then feeling.

steps.text: Ask Sunil to let me lead a pricing report pilot
Keep a file of my finished work for reviews
Add £50 a month to savings for safety

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast to plan for, and I'd want my company and the government to say what they'd do. I'd tell my family the same. I'd also say we shouldn't panic, but I'd mean it only half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be anxious. If AI does most thinking work better and cheaper, a junior analyst is the first thing firms replace. I'd probably still have a job in 2028, but I'd be the kind of person who has to prove daily why a person is cheaper than a program. That's no way to live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd raise my savings to £450 a month by cutting my own spending, and I'd stop sending £80 home unless it's urgent, which would hurt. I'd ask Sunil what skills the company will still pay people for. And I'd look at jobs in underwriting or claims, where there's more contact with customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. It's the first one where my plan, work hard and be useful, is not a plan. I'd keep checking the news, which doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Say it's the day the announcement is made. What do you tell the people close to you that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents, carefully, because they're already worried about Lucia's fees. I'd say don't take on more debt for her, and we'll find a way. Lucia would take it harder; she'd say doctors are safe and I'd say maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what happens to the money you owe and the money you've saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the loan payments the same and put everything else into cash. If I lose my job, I want six months to find another. I'd also ask my parents whether they'd mind my moving back for a stretch, which I'd hate but would do.

say: I'd say it's too fast to plan and want the **company** and government to say their plans.
I'd tell my family not to **panic**, though I'd only half mean it.
I'd ask Sunil what **skills** the company will still pay for.
think: The junior analyst is the first thing firms **replace**.
I'd have to prove daily why a person is **cheaper** than software.
Hard work and being useful are not a **plan** any more.
do: Raise savings to **£450 a month**, even if I stop sending money home.
Look at **underwriting** or claims jobs with customer contact.
Ask my parents if I can **move back** for a stretch.
S2.quote: I'd probably still have a job in 2028, but I'd be the kind of person who has to prove daily why a person is cheaper than a program.
fieldNote: Her plan **hurts**: stopping money to her sister is a real cost.
Looks for **customer contact** work as her hedge.
Telling her **parents** carefully shows how family-bound her worries are.

steps.text: Raise savings to £450 a month by cutting my own costs
Stop sending money home unless it's an emergency
Apply for an underwriting or claims role with customer contact
Tell my parents not to borrow more for Lucia's fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to do something sensible. I'd ask my company for a skills plan and I'd push colleagues to get trained. I'd also say governments should test retraining on a small scale now, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel more in control than at two years. By 2031 I'd be 27, with some experience, perhaps in underwriting or as a team lead. I'd still be a bit scared, because the point of the scenario is that nothing is certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the actuarial course, then take the next level. I'd move into a role with customers or complex judgement. I'd also use the tools more, and I'd keep saving £350 a month. And I'd talk with Lucia about what her specialism might look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady worry, not a spike. Five years is enough to do real things. I'd just have to do them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes about your plan with 5 years instead of 2?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd rather change my skills than only protect my savings, because skills are what keep paying after the savings run out. The two-year version is mostly about cash. This one is about direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you do you think sees this coming, and who doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My manager sees it, I think, and a couple of the older analysts do. Most of my university friends mostly argue about it online. My dad doesn't, and he's the one I'd have to talk to about money.

say: I'd ask my company for a **skills plan**.
I'd say governments should **test retraining** now, not wait.
think: I'd feel more in **control** than with two years.
By 2031 I'd be 27, perhaps in **underwriting** or leading a team.
Nothing is **certain**, so some fear stays.
do: Finish the actuarial course, then the **next level**.
Move into a role with **customers** or complex judgement.
Save **£350 a month** and talk to Lucia about her future.
S3.quote: With five years I'd rather change my skills than only protect my savings, because skills are what keep paying after the savings run out.
fieldNote: She puts **skills** before cash when time allows.
Observes who **sees it**: her manager does, her dad does not, and he holds the family purse.

steps.text: Take the next-level actuarial exams after this year's course
Move into underwriting where I talk to customers
Talk with Lucia and my parents about her fees and plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long, and the sensible thing is to keep calm and keep learning. At work I'd say we have time to build good processes. I'd tell my friends not to panic and not to ignore it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel mostly fine. By 2036 I'd be 32, probably in a middle role, with maybe a family. I'd worry a bit about what the juniors who come after me will do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study part-time for a professional qualification, change roles once or twice, and keep learning the tools as they become normal. I'd start a pension and an index fund early. And I'd help Lucia out if she needs it when she qualifies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A decade gives me room. I'd like to think I'd use it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what would you start now that you wouldn't with 2 years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather spend a decade learning slowly than spend two years panicking and learning nothing. I'd start with one new skill a year. It's boring advice, but it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At 32, what do you hope your working life looks like, and what could stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 32 I'd hope to lead a small team and have a flat of my own. What could stop me is an economic crash, or the company moving analysis to another country or to software.

say: I'd say ten years is long, so **stay calm** and keep learning.
I'd say we have time to build good **processes**.
I'd tell friends neither to **panic** nor to ignore it.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32 in a **middle role**, with maybe a family.
I'd worry about the **juniors** who follow me.
A decade gives me **room**, if I use it.
do: Learn each new tool as it becomes **normal**.
Start a **pension** and an index fund early.
feel: A little **hope** that I would use the time well.
S4.quote: I'd rather spend a decade learning slowly than spend two years panicking and learning nothing.
fieldNote: Her steady style suits a **long** timeline.
The advice is **boring** and she knows it.
Risk named is a **crash** or outsourcing of analysis, not AI alone, which is a fair reading.

steps.text: Study part-time for a professional finance qualification
Learn each new tool once colleagues start using it
Put £150 a month into an index fund
Offer to help Lucia with costs when she qualifies

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time and my family is already stretched. What would help is the company saying plainly what it plans to do, paid training, and some support for families who've already taken on debt for education. Evidence, not slogans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say I'd like people to be less certain about all this. Nobody knows how fast it goes, so a sensible plan has to work if the answer is slow and also if the answer is fast. That's how I try to live.

headlineQuote: Nobody knows how fast it goes, so a sensible plan has to work if the answer is slow and also if the answer is fast.
portrait: Uma is a **22-year-old** junior financial analyst at an insurer, top of her year, sending money home for her sister's medical fees.
She uses AI now and then and wants **evidence** before opinions.
She is centrist and pragmatic, so she blames **no side** and prefers pilots, training and plain plans.
She stays calm in slow worlds, **anxious** at two years, and returns to family money in every answer.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because her family is already stretched and there's no time.
whatWouldHelp: A plain **company plan**, paid training, and support for families who borrowed for education.
